messages.subject: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
messages.subject_clean: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have an issue with a glm model. I want to compare the use of demonstratives this and that in relation to several predictors like CORPUS, POS, POSITION, CONTEXT (endophoric or exophoric) and the 3gram POS tags which constitutes 6 variables: TAG1BEFORE, TAG2BEFORE...TAG1AFTER.

model.01 <-glm(TOKENS~CORPUS+TAGS+CONTEXT+POSITION+TAGS3AFTER+TAGS2AFTER+TAGS1AFTER+TAGS3BEFORE+TAGS2BEFORE+TAGS1BEFORE, data=did.noce.wsj.proforms.determiners.all, family=binomial)

Running it in R throws the above-mentioned message. However, I noticed that if I run the model without the 3gram POS tags I do not get this warning.  After reading a couple of papers it seems that the problem is linked to complete or quasi-complete separation. What I understand is that there are too many levels for each POS tag variable so that some values predict this or that perfectly as they are not repeated many times in the data set. I am wondering if I am on the right track.
If so what should I do? Should I drop these variable from the model? Should I keep them but then how should I compute the significance of the model since the POS tag variables return weird values?

Thanks a lot in advance for any suggestions,

Thomas Gaillat
PhD Student - University of Paris-Diderot - France

messages.subject_clean: Significant factors in a model, but low positive prediction rates
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working right now on a particular morphological alternation. To investigate it I am trying to use logistic regression with mixed effects, but I have a problem. I don't know how I should interpret that some factors in the model are highly significant according to some p value, but the over all model is awful (has no real predictive power)?

If I look at the factors individually there do show a statistically significant, though small, correlation with one or other outcome.

How should I report this? Should I just mention that the model doesn't work, or just ignore this fact and present the correlations individually?

Thank you :)

Best,

Matías Guzmán Naranjo

Hi Thomas,

yes, I have done all that. I have also tried including everything in a random forest just to see if overfitting the model would yield an acceptable confusion matrix, but nothing. One thing I haven't done, but that I am not so sure I should, is equalizing number of observations for each response. As it stands, I have some 1900 observations for one response (let's say A), and 400 for the other (let's say B). What happens with the model is that it just defaults to predicting A in all cases, so I was thinking a possibility would be to only use 400 randomly chosen observations of A and see what happens, but I am not sure this is acceptable.

Best,

Matías

Hi all and Matias,

It seems we are trying to do similar stuff. I have observations of three corpora but not the same number of observations per corpus. Corpus is an independent variable in my model. The results I get are the opposite from yours. I get a significant p-value for one predictor only but the overall model's p-value shows high significance. I am thinking about trying to make a sample where I have the same number of randomly chosen observations per corpus. My intuition is that the uneven number of observations impacts the model but I am not sure. So if anyone has any idea, it would be great.
Thanks in advance,
Thomas
